definition: Data integration is the process of combining, sharing, or synchronizing data from multiple sources to provide users with a unified view.
details: There are a wide range of possible applications for data integration, from commercial (such as when a business merges multiple databases) to scientific (combining research data from different bioinformatics repositories). The decision to integrate data tends to arise when the volume, complexity (that is, big data) and need to share existing data explodes. It has become the focus of extensive theoretical work, and numerous open problems remain unsolved. Data integration encourages collaboration between internal as well as external users. The data being integrated must be received from a heterogeneous database system and transformed to a single coherent data store that provides synchronous data across a network of files for clients. A common use of data integration is in data mining when analyzing and extracting information from existing databases that can be useful for Business information.

explainer.lead: Data integration brings data from different sources together so people can work with one coherent view instead of reconciling each source separately. It matters when growing volumes of complex data need to be shared across a business or research community.

tiers.eli5: Imagine keeping your drawings in several boxes, with each box using different labels. Data integration is like sorting them into one well-organized collection so everyone can find what they need. It helps people share information and work together.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers apply data integration when merging business databases, combining research repositories, or preparing existing databases for data mining. Data is received from heterogeneous database systems, transformed into a single coherent data store, and made available synchronously to clients across a network of files. The main challenges are the heterogeneity and complexity of the sources and the need to keep the shared data coherent.
tiers.paperLevel: Given heterogeneous sources S1, ..., Sn, data integration transforms and combines their data into a coherent store D that provides users with a unified, synchronized view. The problem is driven by increasing data volume, complexity, and sharing requirements. It has received extensive theoretical study, and numerous open problems remain unsolved.

explainer.example: A business merges its customer, sales, and support databases. Their data is transformed into one coherent store, allowing staff to work from a unified, synchronized view rather than checking each database independently.

usedIn.detail: Research data from different bioinformatics repositories is combined for scientific use.

usedIn.name: Data mining
usedIn.detail: Existing databases are integrated so useful business information can be analyzed and extracted.

explainer.intuition: Separate sources may hold useful pieces of the same overall picture, but their differences make them hard to use together. Integration transforms those pieces into a coherent shared store, giving internal and external users a common basis for collaboration.
howItWorks: Identify the multiple data sources that need to be combined, shared, or synchronized.
Receive the data from the heterogeneous database systems.
Transform the data so it fits a single coherent form.
Bring it together in a coherent data store with a unified view.
Provide synchronous data across the network of files for clients.
explainer.whyItMatters: Integration lets people analyze and share information that would otherwise remain fragmented across sources. It supports collaboration between internal and external users and becomes especially important as data volume, complexity, and sharing needs grow.
misconceptions: It is not merely copying data into one place; heterogeneous data must also be transformed into a coherent form.
It is not limited to commercial databases; scientific repositories and data-mining work also use it.
Combining the data is not the whole task; clients also need synchronous access to the shared data.
